By: Johann Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
While the country is burning the public broadcaster prefers that we don't know about it.

Summary:
On 26 May the SABC announced that, with immediate effect, they will no longer show any community protests where government property is being damaged. This has lead to widespread international condemnation of the public broadcaster, to pending court cases and to the dismissal of at least 7 journalists so far. In the mean time we've had an average of about 3 violent protests per day in South Africa. Some say that the country is burning.But what was the rationale for this decision - is there not perhaps some truth that in the reasoning that the mere presence of tv cameras further instigate violence, and that the broadcasting of these images will breed more protests. We will speak to a number of experts on media freedom, the role of the media in fuelling violence etc...

Extra Budget Items:
Apart from the two days with presenter, a cameraman was sent to Riversleigh today to film the protests there. Another cameraman is being sent to Watervalboven to interview Walther da Costa tomorrow. As the person who heads the UN mission on refugees and violence in townships, he is the best person to give a perspective on how many and how violent these protests are.

Press Release:


Service Delivery Time Bomb
The SABC’s controversial decision not to show images of violent service delivery protests sent shock waves through the country. But with several service delivery protests throughout the country every single day, it is clear that frustrations voiced through often violent protests cannot be ignored. An interdict by the Helen Suzman Foundation this week forced the public broadcaster to backtrack on its decision. Carte Blanche asks: are South Africans aware of the magnitude of this ticking time bomb?


Script:


V/o Service delivery protests have become a staple part of our daily news diet. In the big metropoles we have even become used to traffic reports advising us to avoid particular routes due to protest action, much in the same way we've become accustomed to road works or broken traffic lights.
V/o Walter da Costa Er Silva runs a community driven NGO, training volunteers in the townships and rural areas in disaster management and social cohee/sion issues. They also intensively monitor violent protests. His protest alert forum is used by everyone from the media to the police. He says government’s current way of dealing with the protests is not really working.
Walter Mostly it's cordoning off the areas where the protests are taking place and allowing that to completely burn itself out at the end of the day. And that's not bringing things under control. I really think that we are sitting on a time bomb, which way it's going to turn we don't know at this stage – it can go any other way. But definitely that we are having what is normally classified as low intensive conflict on the ground, it is happening there.
V/o "Different sources cite vastly different stats on how many of these protests there actually are, but everyone agrees that the amount of protests and especially the violent ones, are increasing year on year.
Service delivery protests spike in election years.
In 1996 there were 26 violent protests.
In 2009 there were 204
In 2014 the number of violent protests had grown to 218
Now, it's not even two years later and Walter's stats show that 2014's figures have already doubled, and we're only in July. "
Walter From January until now we've monitored – and this is by no means all the protests that have taken place, or even all the violent protests that have taken place – we've monitored around 430 plus protests this year.
V/o That is more than 2 violent protests every day this year. And only 1 in ten protests turn violent.
Many experts are saying the country is literally on fire, but the majority of South Africans seem oblivious to this time bomb, as Walter calls it, and it seems someone wants to keep it that way...
Link Devi 80% of South Africans are dependent on our public broadcaster, the SABC for all it's news and information. And in the past few months more and more voices have been saying they are failing in their primary duty.
V/o In May, the SABC announced that, amongst other changes, they would no longer cover violent protests. Many considered this change in editorial policy to be a deliberate political attempt to misinform voters before the elections on the real state of the nation. The minister of communications remained silent but civil society reacted strongly.
V/o Deputy Vice-Chancellor of Wits, Prof Tawana Kupe also chairs the SOS Support Public broadcasting campaign, and he is concerned that the public broadcaster is being turned back into the sort of state broadcaster that the SABC was during apartheid in the 1980's.
Prof Kupe The difference is the following: The public Broadcaster, it's orientation or posture is towards the public, not any political party or any sectional interest, commercial, religious or social. A state broadcaster is controlled by the particular party that runs the government on that day. It basically sees it as a megaphone, it's his master's voice, if you like. So, right now these kinds of editorial decisions that have been taken by the SABC move it way, a long way of from being a public broadcaster towards being a state broadcaster.
V/o The Right2Know campaign has also joined the fight.
Micha Reddy The SABC, in terms of its mandate, has an obligation to inform the public, and you can't be informing the public if you are doctoring the news and pretending that certain realities – important realities – don't exist. If you are peddling sunshine journalism and 70% good news – that is outright censorship. And we saw what happened in Tshwane recently, when Tshwane was up in flames, media outlets around the country had their cameras focussed on what was happening but the SABC cameras turned away.
V/o And, as we get closer to the elections, the fight stepped up a notch. On the 11th of July the broadcast regulating authority, ICASA, ordered the SABC to withdraw its ban on showing violent protests. Hlaudi Motsoeneng reacted by saying no-one will tell them what to do and that they will go to the highest court over the issue. He suspended 8 of his senior journalists for being critical of his decision. SANEF, the national editors forum responded by awarding the SABC 8 (as they quickly became known), with the prestigious Nat Nakasa award for excellence in journalism. On Monday and Tuesday this week the SABC retaliated by firing all 8 journalists. On Wednesday the Helen Suzman Foundation went to court and won an interim interdict against the SABC, with the court ordering the corporation to reverse the policy changes.
HSF If the SABC violates the interdict we will take it back to court and my hope is that we will be able to sue them, not only within their official capacities but also in their private capacities. And that may hurt them. And if that's the only way they can come to the party, then that's it.
V/o 2 hours later the SABC informed ICASA that they would also comply with their order. On Thursday and Friday 4 of the SABC8 approached the labour court, asking to be re-instated. A public donor page, started on the web on Tuesday to help the now unemployed journos, had already raised R360 000 by then. The court will pass down its verdict tomorrow.....
V/o But many critics are concerned that the battle for control of the public broadcaster is far from over, and that the censorship will now simply move underground, under the guise that these stories are not newsworthy.
Wits Censorship always has a negative impact on society. It undermines freedom of expression which is crucial to running a normal society.
R2K We need to say to politicians hands off the SABC, stop with appointing political lackeys and so on and so forth. This is our public broadcaster, it's supposed to be downwardly accountable, it has a public mandate and it is a key institution of democracy.
V/o And, while all this was going on, the violent protests continued this week, with at least two journalists attacked while covering them, and the time-bomb carries on ticking...
V/o Dr Carin Roon/ciman of UJ's Centre for Social Change is one of many researchers trying to understand why we're in an almost permanent state of protest.
Carin And of course one of the key components there has been the global economic crisis and its impact on SA – loss of jobs, deepening poverty and inequality. And I think that is really how we have to understand these protests as being an expression of poverty and deep inequality and the fact that this has not been changing in any significant way since the beginning of our democracy.
Walter I think the best strategy to follow is to give these people what they really want. People see the amount of money which is being spent on things which are not supposed to be done. They still have to struggle to go fetch a bombozi full of water at a tap and they're not getting electricity, they're not getting water, they're not getting any services. Really getting down and doing the work and showing the work is being done, I think things will stabilise. That's what they are looking for.

10sec Promo So far we've had an average of 2 violent protests every day this year. But, thanks to the SABC, many South Africans are not aware of this.

15sec A "Civil Society strikes back against the SABC's decision to censor the news...
UPSOUND MICHA: It is our We need to say to the SABC
SABC...what is the right thing to do?"

15sec B "Is the SABC playing the violin while South Africa is burning?
UPSOUND MICHA: Sunshine journalism
Is our public broadcaster turning into a state broadcaster?"
